newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Stakes high for Russia in Belarus crisis.
newsitem.headline: Stakes high for Russia in Belarus crisis.

text.p: The crisis in Belarus poses a difficult policy challenge for Russia in which the stakes are high and the Kremlin has little to gain, independent Russian analysts said on Wednesday.

Russia has expressed concern and called for compromise but has been careful not to commit itself openly to one side in the standoff between Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko and parliament over his planned referendum on increasing his powers.
"There is no best option for Russia in this crisis. All it can hope for is damage limitation," said Sergei Karaganov, a respected foreign policy expert who is close to Kremlin thinking.

Russia has set integration with Belarus as a major foreign policy goal. Lukashenko, who signed an agreement with President Boris Yeltsin on April 2 to create a tight-knit alliance between the two former Soviet republics, is central to those plans.
But Lukashenko's autocratic ways have become hard for the Kremlin to swallow, prompting it to slow integration moves and keep a safe distance from Lukashenko as he becomes more isolated.

"Russia is in a very ambiguous position. Lukashenko is a man who calls for union with Russia and espouses the feelings of the majority in Belarus, but he does so in a way which discredits him," Karaganov told Reuters.

The crisis is all the more difficult for Yeltsin because of embarrassing parallels with his own battle with parliament in 1993 which ended in him using tanks to end the resistance of hardliners who had occupied the Moscow parliament building.

"One reason Russia is unwilling to criticise Lukashenko is that he's trying to do what Yeltsin did in 1993 -- consolidate power to break out of a confrontation between the executive and legislative branches of power," said analyst Andrei Kortunov.

Lukashenko wants to increase his rule by more than two years and extend his powers over all institutions. His plans have been criticised by Western leaders and the Belarus parliament wants the referendum, set for Sunday, cancelled.

Kortunov said Moscow's best hope was that the situation would calm down or a compromise be reached which preserved stability. This is vital for integration with a state which Moscow regards as a bridge to the West and a buffer zone against any potential threat.

"Belarus is very important to Russia and the stakes are high. It is a natural gateway to the West, is already deeply integrated with Russia's economy and there are good ties between the two societies," said Kortunov, head of the Russian Science Foundation think tank.
"Whoever emerges as a winner from this crisis, the most important thing for Russia is to see Belarus stable and hope it doesn't collapse into civil chaos," he said.
Lukashenko remains dependent on Russia, his main foreign ally, and Yeltsin spoke to him by telephone on Wednesday in a sign that Moscow may be ready to play a major role in dissolving the crisis.

Integration with Russia's fellow Slavs in Belarus, a country of 10 million people, is regarded by some analysts as costly because Russia would have to absorb its western neighbour's economic problems.

But the Kremlin sees political and strategic benefits from closer ties with Belarus. Integration, the terms of which remain hazy, would go some way to satisfying the desire of some Russians and Belarussians to rebuild the Soviet Union.

Yeltsin used the integration agreement with Belarus last April to boost his re-election campaign after the opposition communists tried to win votes by criticising the agreement which buried the Soviet Union in 1991.
But few concrete steps have been taken since April and Lukashenko won no open promises of quick progress when he addressed parliament in Moscow last week.
"Russia is being very restrained, waiting to see what happens in Belarus", said Irina Kobrinskaya, with the Moscow office of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

"Russia has made a genuine declaration of intent on integration but the fact that nothing has really been done on it since April shows that Moscow has not openly committed itself to Lukashenko. It reserves the right to "deviations' depending on how the situation goes."
